In times of crisis, the instinct for many leaders is to grasp for control. The fear of the unknown, the pressure to deliver answers, and the weight of responsibility can cause even the most seasoned leaders to react with urgency that borders on panic. But control when driving by fear is rarely effective. What people truly need in the middle of chaos is not dominance or micromanages every step. They need someone who can remain calm because calm is contagious. And in a storm, people look for stability more than they look for solutions. Remaining calm doesn't mean being passive or disconnected. It means having the emotional discipline to regulate your response so that others can regulate theirs.

When a leader enters a room during a crisis and speaks in a measured tone, listens intently and asks thoughtful questions that change the entire emotional temperature of the team. Calmness provides psychological safety. It signals to others that while the situation might be uncertain, they are not alone and they are not lost. It becomes a source of collective strength. Crisis often distort time. There's a tendency to believe that every decision must be made immediately. Every issue resolved instantly. This urgency can push readers into reactive mode, making impulsive choices, delivering incomplete messages, or simply acting without full context.

Calmness challenges that impulse. It buys time not by delaying action, but by prioritizing the pause between stimulus and response. That pause is where wisdom lives. It's where the leader assesses not just what's happening, but how people are being affected, what the long-term consequences might be, and which decision aligns with values, not just pressure. There's also a psychological mirror effect in teams. People reflect the emotional state of the leader. If a leader is visibly anxious, snapping at others or rushing without clarity, the team absorbs energy. It multiplies uncertainty and paralyzes initiative.

But when a leader speaks slowly, stays focused, and listens before reacting, it creates an unspoken permission for others to do the same. Calm behavior reinforces the idea that while the crisis may be real, it is not the end as manageable. This doesn't remove the difficulty of the moment, but it equips the team to face it more effectively. One of the great misconceptions about calm leadership is that it's passive or disengaged. That's not true. It takes immense inner strength to be calm when everything around you is in flux. It requires emotional intelligence, self-awareness, and maturity. Calm leaders do not pretend everything is fine.

They acknowledge the gravity of the moment. They just refuse to let fear lead the way. Their steadiness becomes the round others can stand on. It's important to note that calm is not always a natural state, especially in high pressure environments. It must be practiced. Leaders who consistently lead with calm have usually developed routines or habits that keep them grounded. They might have a mental checklist they run through during a crisis. They might take a moment for deep breaths before walking into a room or a meeting. They prepare themselves not just with facts and plan with emotional per readiness.

It's not about intention. They lead their own nervous systems before they try to lead anyone else. Calm also opens the door to empathy. In a crisis, people are not just dealing with logistics. They're managing fear, stress, confusion, and sometimes grief. calm leader creates space for those emotions. They don't rush people past their experience just to check a box or hit a deadline. They recognize that in order to move forward, people first need to feel seen and heard. Calmness in this way becomes a form of care. It says, "I see you. We're going to get through this together." When calm becomes a leader's default response, it fosters a culture of pressure doesn't break people, reveals their strength.

It builds trust because people believe that even that even in the worst of times, their leader won't abandon them to chow. And it models a kind of leadership that doesn't just survive crisis. Calm transforms through. It doesn't mean you have all the answers. It means you have the presence to hold space for others while you find them together. That presence is more powerful than any command. In the midst of crisis, when confusion is high and the stakes are even higher, clarity becomes a leader's most valuable tool. People don't need all the answers to feel safe. They need to understand what's happening, why it matters, and what's expected of them.

Clarity builds trust because it removes the shadows where fear and speculation grow. When a leader communicates with precision and transparency, it gives people something solid to hold to an otherwise unstable environment. In those moments, clarity becomes more than just a communication skill. It becomes an act of leadership. Trust is rarely built in grand gestures. During calm seasons, it is built in the fire. When people are scared and unsure, and they look to the top for guidance. In those moments, if the message is vague, inconsistent, or withheld, people begin to doubt. They question not only the information, but the intentions behind it.

Are we being told the truth? Are decisions being made behind closed doors? Are we being set up to fail? These questions don't surface because people are cynical. They surface because clarity hasn't taken the lead. Trust deteriorates when information is scarce or unclear. It thrives when people are brought into the process, even if the process itself is still messy. A common mistake leaders make under pressure is trying to present a polished but perfect message. But the truth is people don't need perfect. They need honest. They need to hear what is known, what is still unknown and what the path forward might look like.

Even if it's uncertain. Clarity does not mean having all the answers. It means clearly communicating what you know what you're doing about it and what you need from your team. It means making complexity feel navigable. When people see where they fit in the bigger picture, they stop feeling like standards and start feeling like contributors. That sense of agency restores a measure of control and with it a sense of trust. Clarity is also not just about language. It's about alignment. What you say must match what you do. If a leader speaks of unity and collaboration, but then isolates decision-making or favors a few, clarity is lost.

The message may have sound good, but the behavior told a different story. Trust can only survive when the message and the method match. People listen not just to what leaders say, but how they act in difficult moments. Consistency becomes a form of clarity. The most effective leaders create space for feedback, for questions, for concerns to be voiced, and they respond not with dismissiveness, but with understanding.

When people know their voices are heard, when they know their leaders are willing to explain and engage, trust deepens. Clarity becomes a dialogue that reinforces shared understanding. It shows respect and respect is a powerful trust builder. In caotic times, details matter. Ambiguity can breed anxiety. Saying instead of by Friday leaves room for interpretation, saying we're exploring options without saying what those options are leave for doubt. Clarity involves renaming specifics, even if those specifics might change later. It's better to be clear about current realities and adjust when needed than to leave people guessing.

Uncertainty is part of any crisis, but unclear communication should not be. Clarity also empowers others to act. When team members know what the priorities are, what the boundaries are, and what success looks like in this moment, they are far more likely to make good decisions on their own. They aren't paralyzed by fear of doing the wrong thing. They aren't waiting for more direction. Clarity distributes confidence, enables faster, smarter action because it removes the fog from the path ahead. What's often misunderstood is that clarity is not about oversimplifying or sugar quitting the truth. It's about taking complexity and breaking it down in a way that people can understand and use.

It's about removing noise and sharpening focus. When a leader is clear, people can align, they can contribute, they can trust. Because in that clarity, they see not only the challenge, but the leader's willingness to face it head-on. That breeds confidence. And confidence breeds cohesion. And in any crisis, a unified, and formed team will always outperform a scattered, confused one. Clarity isn't just what you give to others. It's what you stand on as a leader when everything else is shaking. When crisis hits, panic is in the first emotion to rise to the surface. It's a natural response to unperved danger, a surge of adrenaline that demands immediate action.

But while panic may be instinctive, it is rarely productive. In fact, it clouds judgment, narrows thinking, and disrupts the very systems we rely on to move through challenge effectively. What cuts through panic is not pressure, not control, but purpose. Purpose is the internal compass that reminds people why they started what they're fighting for and what truly matters. It doesn't remove fear, but it puts it in perspective. And in crisis, perspective is everything. Purpose brings coherence to chaos. It gives people a reason to keep going when outcomes or uncertain resources are stretched. When leaders bring teams back to to purpose, they offer more than motivation.

They offer meaning. Meaning is stronger than fear. When people know why their work matters, they are more likely to endure discomfort, make sacrifices, and collaborate under strain. It divides people. Purpose connects them. It unites them under a shared story that is bigger than the crisis itself. Great leaders know that reminding people of purpose is not about slogans or empty pep talks. It's about anchoring the present in something deeply human and emotionally resonant. During a crisis, the mission doesn't become less important. It becomes more urgent. Purpose rise to the forefront of every conversation, every decision, every action.

When people start to spiral into worry or doubt, the leader brings them back to the why. Why does this work matter right now? Who are we serving? What's at stake if we give into fear? This is especially critical because citricus is in high pressure situations, the human mind tends to focus on threat. Our natural response is to look for danger and avoid loss. But if all people see as what might go wrong, they will begin to lose hope and energy. Purpose reframes the narrative. It shifts attention from fear of failure to the value of impact. Instead of asking what everything falls apart, purpose asks, "What if we rise to the moment and make a difference?" That question changes the energy in the room.

It invites courage. Purpose also acts as a filter for decision-making. In crisis, leaders face dozens of choices every day. Often with incomplete information and intense press, easy to get lost in short-term fixes or reactive tactics. But when a leader is grounded in purpose, it becomes easier to identify which decisions align with core values and long-term goals. It's not about being rigid. It's not being rooted. When leaders return to purpose, they prevent panic from distorting priorities. They focus not just urgent, but on what's essential. Another powerful aspect of purpose is its ability to activate intrinsic motivation.

When people feel they're part of something meaningful, they don't just show up, they bring their best. They think more creatively, collaborate more generously, and take ownership with more pride. In contrast, shuts down innovation, reduces people to survival mode. A purpose-driven environment invites them to stay connected emotionally and mentally even when conditions are difficult. It reminds them that their role matters, that their effort has impact. Leaders who lead with purpose also create a sense of continuity. Crisis can make people feel like everything is falling apart. But when a leader says, "This is who we are.

This is what we stand for." And that hasn't changed. It provides continuity in the face of disruption, that consistency is a stabilizer. It offers people something to believe in when the future feels uncertain. And it says, "We may be shaken, but we're not lost. We still know why we're here. Importantly, purpose doesn't make the crisis easier, but it makes it worth enduring. It gives people a story to tell about the hardship. It turns the crisis into a chapter in a larger narrative of resilience, values, and mission. People remember how they felt in hard times. And when they look back, they will remember whether they're part of something meaningful or merely reacting to chaos.

Leaders who lead with purpose ensure that their teams come out not just surviving the crisis, but transformed by it, more connected to the reason they began the journey in the first place. In the end, the most effective way to overcome panic is not to suppress it, but to overwhelm it with purpose. To lead under pressure is to lead with vision that reaches beyond the moment. When purpose becomes a center of the response, it lifts people out of fear and to focus. It gives them a reason not just to endure the storm, but to move through it with clarity, courage, and conviction. In moments of crisis, the instinct to tighten control can be overwhelming.

Leaders often feel the pressure to make every decision, oversee every task, and direct every move. After all, when the stakes are high, it feels safer to grip the wheel tightly. But real leadership under pressure is not about commanding every action. It's about empowering people to rise. Empowerment builds strength in the team, creates agility in the response, and fosters trust that outlast crisis itself. While command may bring short-term order, empowerment fuels long-term resilience. When people are empowered, they don't just wait for instructions. They step into ownership. They bring their full capacity, creativity, and in commitment to the table.

In high press situations, a single leader can see or do everything. That's why empowerment matters so much. It distributes leadership across the team. It means that the person closest to the problem is trusted to help solve it. It means that decisions can be made in real time by those who have the most context without waiting for top- down approval that may be delayed or disconnected. Empowerment also changes how people feel about the role of the crisis. When a team feels commanded, they tend to retreat into compliance, doing only what's asked, nothing more. They become focused on not making mistakes rather than making a difference.

Fear of failure starts to shape behavior and innovation slows to a crawl. But when people are empowered, they feel trusted and trust breeds confidence. Confident people take initiative. They ask better questions. They see more possibilities. They care more deeply about the outcome because they see themselves as part of the solution. not just as tools to be directed. Empowering others doesn't mean letting go of standards or structure. It means shifting from a model of control to one of enablement. The leader still sets the direction, defines the purpose, and establishes the guardrails. But within that framework, individuals are encouraged to think, act, and lead.

The leader becomes a coach rather than a commander, supporting, challenging, and believing in the team's capacity. This shift is not always easy. It requires humility and trust. It means accepting that others may approach problems differently, and that different doesn't mean wrong. One of the myths of leadership in crisis is that the loudest voice or the fastest decision maker is the strongest leader. But leadership isn't about noise. It's about impact. Some of the most powerful leadership happens when a team member steps forward, takes responsibility, and makes a difference because they were given the space to do so.

Empowerment multiplies the number of leaders in the room. It doesn't diminish leaders authority. It amplify influence by turning leadership into a shared endeavor. Another benefit of empowerment is that it strengthens learning and adaptation. When people are given room to act, they encounter challenges firsthand. They learn quickly, they adapt in real time, and they develop skills that stay with them beyond the crisis. If the leader is always commanding, then learning is limited to the leader's own experience. But when leadership is shared, the entire organization grows. Crisis becomes not just a test, but a training ground for future strength.

Empowerment also reinforces dignity. It tells people that they matter, not just for their labor, for their judgment, their ideas, and their instincts. That message is vital during difficult times. When people feel valued, they're more likely to stay engaged even when things get hard. They don't just follow, they invest. And when people are invested, the quality of work improves, the culture strengthens, and the organization becomes more than the sum of its roles. Of course, empowerment requires intentionality. It's not enough to simply step back and hope people rise. Empowerment works when the leader actively equips others with the tools, information and confidence they need to lead clear expectations, timely feedback, and consistent and recognizing effort, not just results.

It means being available without hovering. True empowerment is not passive. It's deeply engaged, but in a way that lifts others rather than overshadowing them. In the most successful teams, empowerment becomes part of the culture, not just the crisis response. People know that they are trusted to act, to think, to lead. And they rise to that trust. They don't wait for permission. They move with purpose. They don't fear mistakes. They learn from them. They don't look up for every answer. They look inward, outward and forward. They operate as partners, not just performers. And that shift from command to empowerment is what turns a crisis from a breakdown into a breakthrough.

In moments of crisis, leadership is not only tested. It is revealed. The pressure to act quickly, to make hard decisions, and to show strength contempt leaders, to shut down emotionally, to detach from the human side of the situation in the name of efficiency or decisiveness. But true leadership is not about choosing between strength and softness. It is about integrating both. The best leaders lead with empathy and decide with courage. They do not see these qualities as opposites but as essential partners in navigating the most difficult moments with humanity and integrity. Empathy begins with the simple act of paying attention.

In times of stress, people are not just managing task. They are carrying fear, uncertainty, frustration, and often personal loss. Leaders who recognize this don't view emotions as obstacles. They view them as information. Empathy means looking beyond perform metrics and project updates to see the person behind the role. It means noticing who is withdrawn, who is overextending themselves, who needs encouragement, and who just needs to be heard. These observations may not change the facts of the crisis, but they change how people feel about facing it. They feel seen and being seen builds loyalty and trust in ways that no directive or strategy ever could.

When a leader leads with empathy, they create a culture where vulnerability is not punished but respected. This doesn't mean the leader carries emotional weight and makes space for it. It means they means they ask how are you really and they listen without rushing to fix. They offer stability not through pretending to have every answer but by acknowledging the shared difficulty and showing they are present for it. Empathy says you're not alone in this and in crisis that message can be the difference between burnout and resilience. Yet empathy alone is not enough. A leader must also make decisions.

Sometimes hard ones that carry risk or impact people in painful ways. This is where courage comes in. Courage is not the absence of fear. It is the willingness to act in spite of it. Courageous leaders don't wait for perfect clarity or universal agreement. They gather the best information available. They consider the consequences and they make the call. Even when the decision may be unpopular even when the cost is personal because they understand that leadership is not about comfort. It's about responsibility. But what makes courageous decision-making powerful is when it is grounded in empathy.

When a leader decides with courage and leads with empathy, people trust the intention behind the action. They may not agree with the outcome, but they understand the care with which it was made. They see that the decision wasn't about ego, fear, or control. It was about doing what was right for the greater good, even if it was hard. That combination, compassion and conviction, is what earns respect. One of the hardest realities of crisis leadership is that not every decision will be perfect. Mistakes will happen. Outcomes will fall short. But if people believe that their leader truly cares about them and has the courage to own their choices, they are far more willing to forgive missteps.

They are more willing to stand beside that leader through uncertainty. It is not built by bravado. It is built by consistency, humility, and heart. Empathy also plays a key role in communication. A leader who understands how people are feeling can speak into those emotions with clarity and care. They don't sugarcoat the truth, but they don't weaponize it either. They don't want honesty with hope. They choose words that inform, but also uplift. And when people hear those words, they don't just process information. They feel connection. They remember that their leader understands the human stakes, not just the operational ones.

Courage, on the other hand, is what keeps a leader from be paralyzed by compassion. It gives them the backbone to do what is necessary, even when it's unpopular. It gives them the stamina to face criticism, to stand firm in the face of resistance and to keep moving forward when the easier path would be to avoid the conflict altogether. Courage transforms empathy from sentiment into action. It ensures that care doesn't become pacivity but instill fuels meaningful leadership. When empathy and courage work together, the result is a leader who is both trusted and respected. A leader who listens with care but acts with resolve.

A leader who sees the people they serve and refuses to be swayed by fear or pressure. In a crisis, that kind of leadership doesn't just get a team through, it changes them. It sets a standard for what leadership can be. Not cold, not reckless, but deeply human and unwaveringly

How to lead in a crisis | The Way We Work, a TED series
TED · 4:34 · 364,691 views
Read transcript · ~867 words · 5 min read

Transcriber: TED Translators Admin Reviewer: Ivana Korom We think of a great leader as the unwavering captain who guides us forward through challenge and complexity. Confident, unwavering leaders, armed with data and past experience have long been celebrated in business and politics alike. But sometimes and certainly now, a crisis comes along that is so new and so urgent that it upends everything we thought we knew. [The Way We Work] [Made possible with the support of Dropbox] One thing we know for sure is that more upheavals are coming. In a completely interconnected world a single political uprising, a viral video, a distant tsunami, or a tiny virus can send shock waves around the world.

Upheaval creates fear, and in the midst of it people crave security, which can incline leaders toward the usual tropes of strength, confidence, constancy, but it won't work. We have to flip the leadership playbook. First, this type of leadership requires communicating with transparency, communicating often. So how can leaders lead when there is so little certainty, so little clarity? Whether you are a CEO, a prime minister, a middle manager or even a head of school, upheaval means you have to ramp up the humility. When what you know is limited, pretending that you have the answers isn't helpful.

Amidst upheaval, leaders must share what they know and admit what they don't know. Paradoxically, that honesty creates more psychological safety for people, not less. For example when the pandemic devastated the airline industry virtually overnight, CEO of Delta Airlines Ed Bastian ramped up employee communication despite having so little clarity about the path ahead, facing truly dire results. At one point in 2020, losing over a hundred million dollars a day, it would have been far easier for Bastian to wait for more information before taking action, but effective leaders during upheaval don't hide in the shadows.

In fact, as Bastian put it, it is far more important to communicate when you don't have the answers than when you do. Second, act with urgency despite incomplete information. Admitting you don't have the answers does not mean avoiding action. While it's natural to want more information, fast action is often the only way to get more information. Worse, inaction leaves people feeling lost and unstable. When New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern laid out a four level alert system very early in the COVID-19 crisis, she lacked information with which to set the level. Despite lacking answers, she did not wait to communicate about the threat with the nation.

At first she set the level at two, only to change it to four two days later as cases rose. That triggered a national lockdown, which no doubt saved countless lives. Later, when cases began to dissipate, she made subsequent decisions reflecting that new information. Third, leaders must hold purpose and values steady, even as goals and situations change. Values can be your guiding light when everything else is up in the air. If you care about customer experience, don't let go of that in times of upheaval. If a core value is health and safety, put that at the center of every decision you make. Now doing this requires being very transparent about what your values are, and in this way, your steadfastness shows not in your plans but in your values.

Prime Minister Ardern's clear purpose all along was protecting human life. Even as the immediate goal shifted from preventing illness to preparing health systems and ultimately to bolstering the economy. And finally, give power away. Our instincts are to hold even more tightly to control in times of upheaval, but it backfires. One of the most effective ways to show leadership, if counterintuitive, is to share power with those around you. Doing this requires asking for help, being clear that you can't do it alone. This also provokes innovation while giving people a sense of meaning. Nothing is worse in a crisis than feeling like there's nothing you can do to help.

We follow this new kind of leader through upheaval, because we have confidence not in their map but in their compass. We believe they've chosen the right direction given the current information, and that they will keep updating. Most of all, we trust them and we want to help them in finding and refinding the path forward.

How to make smart decisions more easily
TED-Ed · 5:16 · 1,932,749 views
Read transcript · ~837 words · 5 min read

In a 2011 study, researchers followed a group of judges deciding whether or not to offer imprisoned individuals a chance at parole. Logically, one might expect things like an imprisoned person’s crime, existing sentence, and current behavior to be the primary considerations. But while those details were duly examined, one variable had a remarkably large impact: the time of day. Imprisoned people who met with the board in the morning were far more likely to receive parole than those whose cases were reviewed in the afternoon, even if their crimes and sentences were practically identical. This finding might seem strange, but the researchers’ explanation was simple: in the afternoon, the judges were likely exhausted.

Specifically, they were experiencing decision fatigue. This kind of cognitive exhaustion occurs after a period of extended decision making and it can make people more impulsive and less confident while making choices. The dangers of decision fatigue are clear in high-stakes scenarios like this study, but it can have a serious impact on our day-to-day lives as well. So what kinds of choices lead us to this state, and what can we do to fight fatigue? Everything our bodies do— whether physical or mental— uses energy. But while it’s unclear exactly what resources are depleted during mental strain, studies have found many individuals seem to have a daily threshold for making decisions.

And once that threshold is met, most people make the conscious choice to “take it easy” and save serious thinking about any new decisions for another day. How quickly you reach this threshold depends on several variables, including the frequency, complexity, and novelty of the decisions you have to make. For example, choosing what to eat for breakfast isn't very taxing. Not only is this decision limited by what's available, it's also a choice you expect to make once a day with fairly low stakes. And even when you’re not quite sure what to eat, the time between this minor decision and the next one should give you ample room to recover whatever cognitive energy you expend.

But let’s imagine something much trickier. For example, your car suddenly breaks down and you need to replace it right away. This is an unexpected, complicated decision with serious consequences. In this case, there are countless options to choose from, and you won't find them all in one place. To make the optimal choice, you’ll need to do hours of thoughtful research to consider the various pros and cons. And since this is a decision you don’t often make, you’ll also have to identify what considerations are most important. The time pressure can add additional stress both during the decision-making process and afterward, as you expend more energy wondering if you would have made a different decision with more time.

After just a single decision of this magnitude, most people would have already reached their decision-making threshold. But in professions where individuals need to make multiple high-stakes decisions every day, decision fatigue can be much more dangerous. Judges, like those in the 2011 study, often encounter difficult decisions back-to-back, with no time to recover. Many researchers are especially concerned about decision fatigue in medicine. Doctors often work long shifts full of life-or-death decisions, and some studies have found that medical workers are much more likely to make critical mistakes when working extended shifts.

Addressing these issues requires institutional changes, but there are much more direct ways most of us can avoid fatigue in our daily lives. One simple strategy is to make fewer daily decisions, tackling your to-do list over multiple days, or even removing some rote decisions from your day altogether. It’s also typically less draining to offer advice on a hard decision than it is to make that choice yourself. So it can be helpful to imagine your decisions as someone else’s before considering how the consequences impact you specifically. Finally, it's essential to remember that not every choice is equally important, and learning how to relax about the small stuff can help you save energy for the decisions that truly matter.
